1.s: God calls to Moses from the tabernacle and explains the burnt offering: an animal without defect, given wholly to God, “a pleasant aroma to Yahweh”.
1.d: The book opens with God speaking from the Tent of Meeting set up at the end of Exodus [[bible:Leviticus 1:1]] [[nabre:leviticus/0]]. Women as well as men brought sacrifices, and only tame animals of the herd or flock could be offered [[nabre:leviticus/1]]. Laying a hand on the animal’s head may have marked it as the worshipper’s own [[nabre:leviticus/1]].

2.s: The grain offering: fine flour, oil and incense, with salt and no yeast, part burned and part given to the priests.
2.d: Grain offerings could stand alone, take the place of an animal for the poor, or go with an animal offering [[nabre:leviticus/2]]. Sharing salt was an ancient sign of friendship and alliance, hence “the salt of the covenant” [[nabre:leviticus/2]] [[bible:Leviticus 2:13]].

3.s: The peace offering, a sacrifice shared as a fellowship meal with God. The fat and blood belong to God.
3.d: The exact meaning of the Hebrew shelamim is unclear; it has been translated “peace”, “well-being”, “gift” or “communion” offering [[nabre:leviticus/3]]. Unlike the burnt offering, most of the meat was eaten by the worshipper, the family and the priests [[nabre:leviticus/3]].

4.s: The sin offering for unintentional sins by the high priest, the whole community, a leader or an ordinary person.
4.d: This offering deals with wrongs done unintentionally [[nabre:leviticus/4]]. The four cases go down in rank from the high priest to an ordinary person: the higher the position, the more deeply the sin affects the sanctuary, which the blood cleanses [[nabre:leviticus/4]]. Hebrews links the burning of these offerings outside the camp to Jesus suffering outside the city gate [[nabre:leviticus/6]] [[bible:Hebrews 13:11-12]].

5.s: Sins needing confession and offerings, with cheaper options for the poor: two doves, or even flour.
5.d: Birds or even flour could replace a lamb for those who were poor [[nabre:leviticus/5]] [[bible:Leviticus 5:7]] [[bible:Leviticus 5:11]]. Mary and Joseph bring two birds after Jesus’s birth [[bible:Luke 2:24]].

6.s: The guilt offering, with repayment plus a fifth for wronging a neighbour; instructions for the priests about the offerings. The fire on the altar must never go out.
6.d: The reparation (guilt) offering is brought mostly for sacrilege [[nabre:leviticus/5]], and wronging a neighbour also requires repaying in full plus a fifth [[bible:Leviticus 6:5]]. The word for “law” in these chapters is torah, which also means “instruction” [[nabre:leviticus/6]]. Zacchaeus promises far more [[bible:Luke 19:8]].

7.s: More rules for the guilt and peace offerings, and the priests’ share. Eating blood is forbidden.
7.d: Being “cut off” from one’s people is a punishment from God that often seems to mean the end of the offender’s family line [[nabre:leviticus/7]]. The ban on eating blood [[bible:Leviticus 7:26-27]] is still asked of Gentile believers in Acts 15:20 [[bible:Acts 15:20]].

8.s: Moses ordains Aaron and his sons with washing, robes, anointing oil and blood placed on ear, thumb and toe.
8.d: Moses acts as priest during the ordination [[nabre:leviticus/8]]. Blood on the ear, thumb and toe stands for the whole body, marking the priests’ passing from an ordinary to a holy state [[nabre:leviticus/8]]. The Urim and Thummim seem to have been used like lots to learn God’s decision [[nabre:leviticus/8]].

9.s: Aaron offers his first sacrifices, blesses the people, and fire from God consumes the offering. The people shout and fall on their faces.
9.d: The eighth day completes the ordination [[nabre:leviticus/9]]. The people are blessed twice; the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:22–27 may show its content [[nabre:leviticus/9]]. Fire from God’s presence shows his glory [[nabre:leviticus/9]], as later at Solomon’s temple [[bible:2 Chronicles 7:1]] and Elijah’s altar [[bible:1 Kings 18:38]].

10.s: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer “strange fire” and are consumed. Priests are told not to drink before serving, and to teach the difference between holy and common.
10.d: Nadab and Abihu’s sin seems to have been using coals from a source God had not approved, instead of from the altar [[nabre:leviticus/10]]. The lesson is that worship done wrongly dishonours God’s holiness [[nabre:leviticus/10]] [[bible:Leviticus 10:3]]. Priests must teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean [[nabre:leviticus/10]] [[bible:Leviticus 10:10]].

11.s: Laws on clean and unclean animals: which land animals, fish, birds and insects may be eaten.
11.d: The reason given for the food laws is holiness: “be holy, for I am holy” [[nabre:leviticus/11]] [[bible:Leviticus 11:44-45]]. Telling clean from unclean animals is compared to God setting Israel apart from the peoples [[nabre:leviticus/11]] [[bible:Leviticus 20:26]]. 1 Peter quotes the command [[bible:1 Peter 1:16]], and the New Testament declares all foods clean [[bible:Mark 7:19]] [[bible:Acts 10:15]].

12.s: Purification after childbirth, with an offering of a lamb, or two birds for the poor.
12.d: There is no simple link in the Bible between a person’s worth and the impurity something causes [[nabre:leviticus/12]]. Circumcision on the eighth day is the sign of the covenant, kept after Jesus’s birth [[nabre:leviticus/12]], and Mary brings the offering of the poor [[bible:Luke 2:22-24]] [[nabre:leviticus/12]].

13.s: How priests are to examine skin diseases and mould, and the isolation of those with infectious conditions.
13.d: The Hebrew tsara’at covers several skin diseases and even mould on cloth and walls; “leprosy” is misleading, as Hansen’s disease is probably not included [[nabre:leviticus/13]]. The sufferer mourned, lived outside the camp and cried “Unclean!” [[nabre:leviticus/13]] [[bible:Leviticus 13:45-46]], yet Jesus touches such a man and heals him [[bible:Mark 1:41]].

14.s: The ceremony for cleansing a healed person, with two birds, one released alive, and for cleansing houses.
14.d: These rites are for cleansing after recovery, not for healing [[nabre:leviticus/14]]. The live bird carries impurity away, like the scapegoat on the Day of Atonement [[nabre:leviticus/14]]. Jesus sends a healed man to the priest to offer what Moses commanded [[bible:Mark 1:44]].

15.s: Bodily discharges and the cleansing needed after them.
15.d: These discharges may count as unclean partly because they involve the loss of fluids of life, at the margins of life and death [[nabre:leviticus/15]]. The rites are for purification, not cure [[nabre:leviticus/15]]. A woman with a chronic flow of blood [[bible:Leviticus 15:25]] is healed by touching Jesus’s clothes [[nabre:leviticus/15]] [[bible:Mark 5:25-29]].

16.s: The Day of Atonement: once a year the high priest enters the Most Holy Place with blood, and a second goat, the scapegoat, carries the people’s sins into the wilderness.
16.d: Only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year [[nabre:leviticus/16]]. The verb kipper, “atone”, means the removal of sin and impurity, and here even deliberate sins are included [[nabre:leviticus/16]]. With both hands the priest transfers the sins onto the goat sent to Azazel, a name for a demon of the wilderness [[nabre:leviticus/16]]. Hebrews uses this day’s imagery for Christ [[nabre:leviticus/16]] [[bible:Hebrews 9:7-12]].

17.s: All sacrifices must be brought to the tabernacle, and no one may eat blood, “for the life of the flesh is in the blood”.
17.d: Every animal slaughtered had to be brought to the sanctuary as an offering; Deuteronomy 12 later allows slaughter at home [[nabre:leviticus/17]]. Atonement by blood here is probably about the guilt of taking an animal’s life [[nabre:leviticus/17]]. Others read the blood as life given up in death, pointing to death as the basis of atonement [[eob:Leviticus]].

18.s: Forbidden sexual relationships, and a warning not to follow the practices of Egypt and Canaan.
18.d: Chapters 17–26 are the “Holiness” laws [[nabre:leviticus/0]], often called the Holiness Code [[eob:Leviticus]], marked by the refrain “I am Yahweh” [[nabre:leviticus/18]]. Chapter 20 repeats most of these cases with penalties [[nabre:leviticus/18]]. John the Baptist rebuked Herod Antipas for breaking 18:16 [[nabre:leviticus/18]] [[bible:Matthew 14:4]].

19.s: “Be holy, for I, Yahweh your God, am holy”: laws about honouring parents, gleaning for the poor, honesty, fairness, and “love your neighbor as yourself”.
19.d: Israel is to be holy by keeping God’s commands [[nabre:leviticus/19]], and leaving gleanings feeds the poor [[nabre:leviticus/19]]. 19:18, “love your neighbor as yourself”, became one of the central commandments in Judaism and Christianity [[nabre:leviticus/19]] [[bible:Matthew 22:39]]; 19:34 asks the same love for the foreigner [[bible:Leviticus 19:34]], and the New Testament adds love for enemies [[nabre:leviticus/19]] [[bible:Matthew 5:44]].

20.s: Penalties for child sacrifice to Molech, sorcery, and sexual sins.
20.d: Molech may have been a god linked with the underworld, worshipped in Judah in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem [[nabre:leviticus/20]]. Why different offences carry different penalties is not clear [[nabre:leviticus/20]].

21.s: Rules of holiness for priests in mourning, marriage and physical fitness for service.
21.d: Priests had to avoid contact with the dead except for close relatives; the high priest could have none [[nabre:leviticus/21]]. A priest with a bodily defect could not serve at the altar but was not unclean and still ate the holy food [[nabre:leviticus/21]] [[bible:Leviticus 21:22]].

22.s: Who may eat holy food, and what animals are acceptable as offerings: without defect.
22.d: Whoever and whatever comes to the altar must be whole [[nabre:leviticus/22]]. Rules such as not killing a mother animal and its young on the same day have a humanitarian tone [[nabre:leviticus/22]] [[bible:Leviticus 22:28]]. 1 Peter calls Christ a lamb without blemish [[bible:1 Peter 1:19]].

23.s: Israel’s calendar of feasts: Sabbath, Passover, unleavened bread, firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Tabernacles.
23.d: Passover and Unleavened Bread were probably separate feasts at first, together celebrating the exodus [[nabre:leviticus/23]]. The feast fifty days later is Pentecost, the feast of Weeks for the wheat harvest [[nabre:leviticus/23]], the day the Spirit came [[bible:Acts 2:1]]. Paul calls the risen Christ “the first fruits” [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:20]].

24.s: Oil for the lamp and bread for the table; a man who blasphemes God’s name is stoned.
24.d: The lamp must burn continually [[bible:Leviticus 24:2]]. The same law applies to the foreigner and the native-born [[bible:Leviticus 24:22]].

25.s: The Sabbath year for the land, and the Jubilee every fiftieth year: land returns to its family, and Israelites in slavery go free.
25.d: In the fiftieth year, the jubilee, land returns to its family and indentured Israelites go home [[nabre:leviticus/25]]; the word jubilee (yobel) means “ram’s horn”, blown to announce it [[nabre:leviticus/25]]. God is the true owner of the land [[bible:Leviticus 25:23]] [[nabre:leviticus/25]]. Foreign slaves, however, were not released [[nabre:leviticus/25]]. Jesus proclaims “the acceptable year of the Lord” [[bible:Luke 4:19]].

26.s: Blessings for obedience, curses for disobedience, and the promise that God will remember his covenant even in exile.
26.d: This chapter ends the laws given at Sinai [[bible:Leviticus 26:46]] [[nabre:leviticus/26]]. Blessings and curses like these also close ancient Near Eastern treaties and Deuteronomy [[nabre:leviticus/26]]. God will remember his covenant when the people repent [[nabre:leviticus/26]], and 26:12 is quoted in 2 Corinthians 6:16 [[bible:2 Corinthians 6:16]].

27.s: Rules for vows, dedications to God and redeeming them, and the tithe.
27.d: A vow is a promise to give something to God if he grants a request [[nabre:leviticus/27]]. Firstborn animals and people already belong to God and cannot be vowed [[nabre:leviticus/27]]. Jesus criticises those who used gifts to God to avoid caring for parents [[bible:Mark 7:11]].
